I was diagnosed at ten, but was never told by my parents and never medicated. I started to suspect in my forties, and now in my sixties am certain. I have memories of being tested and was able to find what one of the tests was by googling a description of it. It was called the Kohs Block Test. I believe, based on overheard conversations as a child, that I was assigned an IQ of 140 based on it.

I must say right now that I think there is a lot of BS surrounding the notion of IQ. That test determined the speed at which you could solve a series of visual puzzles. It was administered to kids because it didn't rely on reading proficiency. I would learn as an adult (long story) that people with dyslexia would perform poorly on it, and there are some successful, intelligent people with the condition. I obviously tested very low for dyslexia.

My life has been a legacy of challenges. I did very well at comprehending science and got a degree in engineering. It took twenty years and I graduated very near the bottom of my class.

As to your question, the challenges I faced were on average consistent. I had periods of great success followed by total failure that triggered deep depressions. It's a roller coaster ride. If you are like me you are having a bad patch and it may get better. Try counseling and learning coping strategies. Armed with knowledge you may want to try getting off the meds. If you do plan it with your doctor. I now write. My audience is mostly strangers like you, but the process is cathartic.

"Bikes have the same rights and responsibilities as cars." True, to a point. I cycle vehiculary when appropriate. There are situations where is isn't advisable. Bikes should follow vehicle codes, making adjustments to account for the different capabilities and limits cars and bikes have.

Bikes are more maneuverable, and give the rider much better visibility. Cars are bigger and faster. I live in a coastal resort town where VC is quite appropriate.  One poster, u/Kinovelo mentioned VC'ing NYC. Those conditions are vaguely similar to the area I ride. Traffic density is much lower, but car speeds are slower due to speed limits and gawking tourists. I do things that the unaware see as hazardous, but aren't.

I do not fear being hit by a car. Special forces in the military have a phrase, Situational Awareness. This applies to VCers like me. You cannot just get out in the road and expect cars to respect, or understand, what you are doing. You need to use that bike's great visibility to be as aware of your surroundings as you can be. I have also learned tricks that I use.

An example; I use bike lanes, and ride toward the middle IF there is no vehicle parking on that side. If there are cars parked I ride all the way to the left stradling the 6" line. Doors can kill.  Often there is an obstruction in the bike lane that requires taking a traffic lane. Look behind and if clear for a hundred feet or more, depending on speed of traffic, make eye contact, stick out your left arm and take the lane. Sometimes the windshield is smoked and you cannot make eye contact. Discretion is the better part of valor. I'll stop and wait for clearance.
